claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies.

claims.claim: Earlier mapped regions in the IPS are strongly engaged only by vision, while higher maps are recruited when participants engage spatial auditory attention.
claims.source: While the earlier mapped regions are strongly engaged only by vision, the higher maps are recruited when participants engage spatial auditory attention (Michalka et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Alpha oscillations (8–14 Hz) are associated with a range of neural functions.
claims.source: Alpha oscillations (8–14 Hz) are associated with a range of neural functions (Klimesch, 2012; Weisz et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Parietal cortex generates strong alpha oscillations measurable using electro- and magneto-encephalography (EEG and MEG).
claims.source: Parietal cortex generates strong alpha oscillations measurable using electro- and magneto-encephalography (EEG and MEG) (Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010; Kelly et al., 2006; Worden et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: When listeners focus visual attention, alpha power lateralizes, increasing in the parietal hemisphere ipsilateral to the direction of attention and decreasing contralaterally.
claims.source: When listeners focus visual attention, alpha power lateralizes, increasing in the parietal hemisphere ipsilateral to the direction of attention and decreasing contralaterally (Kelly et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Auditory spatial attention results in lateralized parietal alpha activity.
claims.source: Auditory spatial attention also results in lateralized parietal alpha activity (Banerjee et al., 2011; Mehraei et al., 2018; Deng et al., 2019; Wöstmann et al., 2016; Frey et al., 2014; Strauß et al., 2014)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Alpha lateralization shifts systematically as the focus of auditory spatial attention shifts from far-left to far-right.
claims.source: indeed, alpha lateralization shifts systematically as the focus of auditory spatial attention shifts from far-left to far-right (Mehraei et al., 2018; Deng et al., 2020) (see Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and reference to Figure 1A showing this pattern.

claims.claim: Focusing spatial attention in both vision and audition leads to similar parietal alpha activity.
claims.source: These results suggest that focusing spatial attention in both vision and audition leads to similar parietal alpha activity.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited research on alpha lateralization in both modalities.

claims.claim: Auditory spatial processing relies on retinotopic regions of parietal cortex, but processing nonspatial features does not, even when listeners are attending the same source in the same sound mixture.
claims.source: While auditory spatial processing relies on retinotopic regions of parietal cortex, processing nonspatial features does not, even when listeners are attending the same source in the same sound mixture (Michalka et al., 2016; Hill and Miller, 2010; Noyce et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: For a target defined by its location, alpha lateralization appears only transiently at the start of a trial if competing streams have distinct nonspatial features.
claims.source: Indeed, for a target defined by its location, alpha lateralization appears only transiently at the start of a trial if competing streams have distinct nonspatial features (Bonacci et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Spatial auditory attention utilizes parietal cortex and produces lateralized alpha.
claims.source: Thus, spatial auditory attention utilizes parietal cortex and produces lateralized alpha
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited research on parietal involvement and alpha lateralization during spatial attention.

claims.claim: Nonspatial auditory attention does not utilize parietal cortex and produces no signature of attentional focus in parietal cortex.
claims.source: however, nonspatial auditory attention does not and produces no signature of attentional focus in parietal cortex.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited research showing lack of parietal involvement in nonspatial attention.

claims.claim: Maintaining attention on an ongoing auditory stream is supported by continuity of features like pitch, location, voice, and timbre.
claims.source: Numerous behavioral studies demonstrate that maintaining attention on an ongoing auditory stream is supported by continuity of features like pitch, location, voice, and timbre (Best et al., 2008; Darwin and Carlyon, 1995).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claims.claim: Feature continuity influences performance automatically: even when listeners know they should ignore some feature, discontinuities in the task-irrelevant feature disrupt attention.
claims.source: Feature continuity influences performance automatically: even when listeners know they should ignore some feature, such as talker identity, and attend to a different feature, such as location, discontinuities in the task-irrelevant feature disrupt attention (Best et al., 2008; Maddox and Shinn-Cunningham, 2012; Bressler et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Effects of talker continuity on speech perception in quiet have been ascribed to 'talker normalization,' but may actually be due to disruptions of attention triggered by a talker change.
claims.source: Indeed, effects of talker continuity on speech perception in quiet have been ascribed to 'talker normalization,' but may actually be due to disruptions of attention triggered by a talker change (Lim et al., 2019; Choi and Perrachione, 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent research reinterpreting prior findings.

claims.claim: Talker discontinuity during an auditory spatial attention task interferes with recall of the target stream and disrupts parietal alpha lateralization.
claims.source: Talker discontinuity during an auditory spatial attention task not only interferes with recall of the target stream, it disrupts parietal alpha lateralization (Mehraei et al., 2018) (see Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research and reference to Figure 1B showing this effect.

claims.claim: In switching trials when listeners were instructed to listen to syllables from one direction (ignoring any talker change), errors were elevated for the syllable right after the talker switch and subsequent alpha lateralization was disrupted.
claims.source: In switching trials when listeners were instructed to listen to syllables from one direction (ignoring any talker change), errors were elevated for the syllable right after the talker switch —and subsequent alpha lateralization was disrupted (see bottom of Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Mehraei et al., 2018) and reference to Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Talker continuity overrides top-down, volitional control of spatial attention; when the talker from the attended location jumps to the opposite side of the listener, the talker discontinuity interrupts spatial attention and parietal alpha lateralization.
claims.source: These results suggest that talker continuity overrides top-down, volitional control of spatial attention; when the talker from the attended location jumps to the opposite side of the listener, the talker discontinuity interrupts spatial attention and parietal alpha lateralization.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the results of Mehraei et al. (2018).

claims.claim: TMS inactivation of parietal cortex in one hemisphere causes spatially specific visual processing changes, enhancing spatial attention directed ipsilaterally but degrading it contralaterally.
claims.source: TMS inactivation of parietal cortex in one hemisphere causes spatially specific visual processing changes, enhancing spatial attention directed ipsilaterally but degrading it contralaterally (Hilgetag et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior TMS research.

claims.claim: Unilateral TMS inactivation of the frontal eye field (FEF) reduces alpha coupling between prefrontal and parietal cortices; moreover, parietal alpha lateralization is disrupted and this disruption predicts increases in reaction times during a visual working memory task.
claims.source: Unilateral TMS inactivation of the frontal eye field (FEF, part of the fronto-parietal visuo-spatial attention network) reduces alpha coupling between prefrontal and parietal cortices; moreover, parietal alpha lateralization is disrupted and this disruption predicts increases in reaction times during a visual working memory task (Sauseng et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior TMS research.

claims.claim: Unilateral 20 Hz rTMS (which disrupts alpha oscillations) of either FEF or parietal cortex has similar effects on alpha coupling and lateralization.
claims.source: Unilateral 20 Hz rTMS (which disrupts alpha oscillations) of either FEF or parietal cortex has similar effects (Capotosto et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior rTMS research.

claims.claim: Alpha-rate rTMS of parietal cortex enhances performance for ipsilateral targets and degrades performance for contralateral targets for visual spatial attention and working memory tasks, while stimulation at non-alpha frequencies has no effect.
claims.source: Alpha-rate rTMS of parietal cortex enhances performance for ipsilateral targets and degrades performance for contralateral targets for visual spatial attention (Romei et al., 2010) and working memory (Sauseng et al., 2009) tasks, while stimulation at non-alpha frequencies has no effect.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior rTMS research.

claims.claim: Two studies failed to find frequency- or retinotopically specific effects of parietal tACS stimulation on visual tasks.
claims.source: Two studies failed to find frequency- or retinotopically specific effects of parietal tACS stimulation on visual tasks (Brignani et al., 2013; Veniero et al., 2017)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior tACS research.

claims.claim: A high-density tACS (HD-tACS) study found that parietal alpha stimulation affects volitional control of visual spatial attention, improving performance for targets ipsilateral to the stimulation.
claims.source: while a high-density tACS (HD-tACS) found that parietal alpha stimulation affects volitional control of visual spatial attention, improving performance for targets ipsilateral to the stimulation (Schuhmann, 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior HD-tACS research.

claims.claim: Stimulation of auditory cortex can influence auditory task performance, including spatially specific effects on auditory selective attention.
claims.source: A few studies have shown that stimulation of auditory cortex can influence auditory task performance (Riecke et al., 2018; Riecke et al., 2015; Zoefel et al., 2018; Neuling et al., 2012), including spatially specific effects on auditory selective attention (Wöstmann et al., 2018; Hanenberg et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on auditory cortex stimulation.

claims.claim: HD-tACS uses an electrode ring configuration (e.g., an anode flanked by multiple cathodes) and creates a more focused electrical current sink compared to traditional tACS.
claims.source: Compared to traditional tACS (conducted through sponge pads), HD-tACS, which uses an electrode ring configuration (e.g., an anode flanked by multiple cathodes), creates a more focused electrical current sink (Kuo et al., 2013; Reinhart and Nguyen, 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on HD-tACS methodology.

claims.claim: HD-tACS allows for more precise anatomical targeting than traditional tACS.
claims.source: This allows for more precise anatomical targeting.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the more focused current sink produced by HD-tACS.

claims.claim: Combined with improved computational models of predicted current flow in the brain, HD-tACS yields more precise brain stimulation than traditional approaches.
claims.source: Combined with improved computational models of predicted current flow in the brain (Datta et al., 2009; Edwards et al., 2013), HD-tACS yields more precise brain stimulation than traditional approaches.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to research on computational modeling and is an inference about the combined benefits.

claims.claim: The study targeted right intraparietal sulcus (rIPS) based on previous findings suggesting that right parietal cortex contains the only representation of left exocentric space, whereas right space is represented strongly in left IPS but also weakly in rIPS.
claims.source: We targeted right intraparietal sulcus (rIPS) based on previous findings suggesting that right parietal cortex contains the only representation of left exocentric space, whereas right space is represented strongly in left IPS but also weakly in rIPS (Farah et al., 1989; Thiebaut de Schotten et al., 2011; Shulman et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on hemispheric asymmetry in spatial representation.

claims.claim: During spatial attention, rIPS alpha stimulation was expected to suppress the representation of left exocentric space, impairing performance for leftward targets.
claims.source: During spatial attention, we expected rIPS alpha stimulation to suppress the representation of left exocentric space, impairing performance for leftward targets (see Figure 3, bottom left panel).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis of the study, based on prior knowledge and depicted in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Performance for rightward targets was hypothesized to either be unchanged (as rIPS should already have strong alpha due to top-down spatial attention) or enhanced (if stimulation led to even better suppression of the leftward distractor).
claims.source: We had a secondary hypothesis that performance for rightward targets might either be unchanged (as rIPS should already have strong alpha due to top-down spatial attention) or enhanced (if stimulation led to even better suppression of the leftward distractor; see Figure 3, bottom right panel).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis of the study, based on reasoning about alpha dynamics and depicted in Figure 3.

claims.claim: When listeners attended to the left, performance changed in the expected direction, dropping from 87.40% correct in continuous trials to 65.29% in switching trials in the main experiment.
claims.source: When listeners attended to the left, performance changed in the expected direction, dropping from 87.40% correct in continuous trials to 65.29% in switching trials (Z(19) = 3.91, Padj <0.001, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claims.claim: When listeners attended to the right, performance dropped from 88.27% for continuous to 64.81% for switching trials in the main experiment.
claims.source: When listeners attended to the right, performance also dropped, from 88.27% for continuous to 64.81% for switching trials (Z(19) = 3.90, Padj <0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claims.claim: When listeners directed attention to a specific talker in the main experiment, the average accuracy dropped slightly for switching compared to continuous trials for both attend-female (79.62% to 79.13%) and attend-male (85.48% to 81.44%) trials.
claims.source: When listeners directed attention to a specific talker, the average accuracy also dropped slightly for switching compared to continuous trials for both attend-female (79.62% to 79.13%) and attend-male (85.48% to 81.44%) trials.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claims.claim: For attend-female trials in the main experiment, the change from continuous to switching was not significant (Z(19) = 0.20, Padj >0.99).
claims.source: For attend-female trials, this change was not significant (Z(19) = 0.20, Padj >0.99)
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claims.claim: For attend-male trials in the main experiment, the change from continuous to switching reached significance (Z(19) = 2.36, Padj = 0.036).

claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claims.claim: In the control experiment, when listeners attended to the left, performance dropped from 79.81% correct in continuous trials to 56.84% correct in the switching trials.
claims.source: When listeners attended to the left, performance dropped as expected, from 79.81% correct in continuous trials to 56.84% correct in the switching trials (Z(17) = 3.66, Padj <0.001, Wilcoxon signed rank test corrected for multiple comparisons).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the control experiment data with statistical support.

claims.claim: In the control experiment, when listeners attended to the right, performance dropped from 80.77% to 57.26%.
claims.source: When listeners attended to the right, performance dropped from 80.77% to 57.26% (Z(17) = 3.71, Padj <0.001).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the control experiment data with statistical support.

claims.claim: In the control experiment, when listeners directed attention to a specific talker, average accuracy was lower for switching than continuous trials for both attend-female (77.35% to 70.51%) and attend-male (74.79% to 70.62%) trials.
claims.source: When listeners directed attention to a specific talker, average accuracy was lower for switching than continuous trials for both attend-female (77.35% to 70.51%) and attend-male (74.79% to 70.62%) trials.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the control experiment data.

claims.claim: In the control experiment, the change from continuous to switching reached statistical significance for the attend-female trials (Z(17) = 2.76, Padj = 0.011), but not the attend-male trials (Z(17) = 1.86, Padj = 0.13).
claims.source: This change reached statistical significance for the attend-female trials (Z(17) = 2.76, Padj = 0.011), but not the attend-male trials (Z(17) = 1.86, Padj = 0.13).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the control experiment data.

claims.claim: The study found a larger drop in performance from continuous to switching trials than in Mehraei et al. (2018), consistent with the fact that talkers switched after each syllable in the current study, which should be more disruptive than a single switch.
claims.source: It is worth noting that our talkers switched after each syllable (see Figure 2B), which should be more disruptive than a single switch (as in Mehraei et al., 2018, which inspired this manipulation). Consistent with this, we found a larger drop in performance from continuous to switching trials than in Mehraei et al. (2018).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the current study's design and results with prior research.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference in baseline performance between Sham and Stimulation sessions in either the main experiment (Z(19) = 0.068, p=0.95) or the control experiment (Z(17) = 0.46, p=0.65).
claims.source: We first confirmed that there was no significant difference in baseline performance between Sham and Stimulation sessions in either the main experiment (Z(19) = 0.068, p=0.95, Wilcoxon rank test) or the control experiment (Z(17) = 0.46, p=0.65, Wilcoxon rank test).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claims.claim: Counter-balancing the session order canceled out any systematic effects of testing order.
claims.source: Thus, counter-balancing the session order canceled out any systematic effects of testing order.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of significant difference in baseline performance between sessions.

claims.claim: Individual subjects' performance across sessions was significantly correlated in both the main experiment (Spearman's Rhos = 0.48; p=0.032) and the control experiment (Spearman's Rhos = 0.52; p=0.028), indicating the stability of individual differences across testing days.
claims.source: We found that individual subjects' performance across sessions was significantly correlated in both the main experiment (Spearman's Rhos = 0.48; p=0.032) and the control experiment (Spearman's Rhos = 0.52; p=0.028), indicating the stability of individual differences across testing days.
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, with an inference about what it indicates.

claims.claim: For rIPS alpha stimulation, performance in the 'stimulation' block was significantly worse in the Stimulation session than in the Sham session for left attention (Z(19) = 2.10, Padj = 0.036).
claims.source: Specifically, for rIPS alpha stimulation, performance in the 'stimulation' block was significantly worse in the Stimulation session than in the Sham session for left attention (Z(19) = 2.10, Padj = 0.036, Wilcoxon signed rank test, corrected for multiple comparisons).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data with statistical support.

claims.claim: There was no significant increase in performance from Sham to Stimulation sessions for right attention (Z(19) = 1.27, Padj > 0.99).
claims.source: There was no significant increase in performance from Sham to Stimulation sessions for right attention (Z(19) = 1.27, Padj > 0.99; see Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data, shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Baseline-corrected performance was consistently lower in the Stimulation session compared to the Sham session for each of the sub-blocks in the 'stimulation' block.
claims.source: We observed a consistent, sustained effect of stimulation: baseline-corrected performance was lower in the Stimulation session compared to the Sham session for each of the sub-blocks in the 'stimulation' block (left side of Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from post hoc analysis of the experimental data, shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The difference in performance between Stimulation and Sham sessions disappeared by the first post-stimulation sub-block, immediately after HD-tACS stopped.

claims.evidence: This is a finding from post hoc analysis of the experimental data, shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Of the 32 distinct trial types, Sham vs. Stimulation sessions differed significantly only in one, in the expected direction: during alpha stimulation of rIPS, when listeners directed spatial attention to a continuous-talker target that was on the left.
claims.source: Of the 32 distinct trial types, Sham vs. Stimulation sessions differed significantly only in one, in the expected direction: during alpha stimulation of rIPS, when listeners directed spatial attention to a continuous-talker target that was on the left (top leftmost panel in Figure 7A, repeated from Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the statistical analyses across all conditions, referencing Figure 7A.

claims.claim: There was no effect of theta stimulation for any of the 16 trial types in the control experiment: for all of these, Z(17) < 1.67 (p>0.095).
claims.source: In addition, there was no effect of theta stimulation for any of the 16 trial types in the control experiment [(spatial and nonspatial attention) x (during stimulation and post stimulation) x (continuous trials and switching trials) x (left/female and right/male)]: for all of these, Z(17) < 1.67 (p>0.095).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of statistical results from the control experiment.

claims.claim: Comparing baseline-corrected performance for Sham vs. Stimulation sessions during nonspatial attention, there was no effect of stimulation for targets from either the left (Z(19) = 0.23, p=0.82) or the right (Z(19) = 1.30, p=0.19).
claims.source: Comparing baseline-corrected performance for Sham vs. Stimulation sessions during nonspatial attention, we observed no effect of stimulation for targets from either the left (Z(19) = 0.23, p=0.82) or the right (Z(19) = 1.30, p=0.19).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc analysis of the experimental data.

claims.claim: The lack of effect of parietal stimulation on nonspatial attention trials (even when analyzed by target location) further supports the view that alpha stimulation of parietal cortex only influences top-down spatial processing.
claims.source: These results further support the view that alpha stimulation of parietal cortex only influences top-down spatial processing.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of stimulation effects during nonspatial attention.

claims.claim: The study shows a causal relationship between parietal alpha power and spatial auditory attention using HD-tACS to stimulate rIPS.
claims.source: Using HD-tACS to stimulate rIPS, we here show a causal relationship between parietal alpha power and spatial auditory attention.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data.

claims.claim: Right HD-tACS parietal stimulation disrupted selective attention directed to the left.
claims.source: We found that right HD-tACS parietal stimulation disrupted selective attention directed to the left.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claims.claim: There was no effect of parietal stimulation on performance when listeners focused top-down attention based on talker identity, when the talker in the attended direction switched abruptly, or when theta stimulation was employed.
claims.source: We found no effect on performance in the myriad control conditions (i.e., when listeners focused top-down attention based on talker identity, when the talker in the attended direction switched abruptly, or when theta stimulation was employed).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from the control conditions in the experimental data.

claims.claim: Alpha HD-tACS stimulation produced an effect size of 0.33 for leftward spatial attention, which is comparable to those in past published reports of tACS effects on cognitive function in healthy adults (Ē=0.36, 95% CI = 0.27–0.46) as well as tDCS studies (e.g., Ē = 0.23, 95% CI = 0.09–0.36).
claims.source: In our study, alpha HD-tACS stimulation produced an effect size of 0.33 for leftward spatial attention. A meta-analysis study (Schutter and Wischnewski, 2016) shows that this effect size is comparable to those in past published reports of tACS effects on cognitive function in healthy adults (Ē=0.36, 95% CI = 0.27–0.46) as well as tDCS studies (e.g., Ē = 0.23, 95% CI = 0.09–0.36) (Brunoni and Vanderhasselt, 2014; Hill et al., 2016; Klaus and Schutter, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of the current study's effect size with those reported in prior meta-analyses.

claims.claim: The frequency specificity of HD-tACS parietal stimulation (alpha but not theta) implicates alpha in control of auditory spatial attention.
claims.source: This frequency specificity of HD-tACS parietal stimulation implicates alpha in control of auditory spatial attention.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential effects of alpha vs. theta stimulation.

claims.claim: The spatial specificity of the effect of rIPS stimulation (affecting left but not right attention) is consistent with the hypothesis that parietal alpha causally suppresses the representation of contralateral space, steering spatial attention.
claims.source: Regardless, the spatial specificity of the effect of rIPS stimulation is consistent with the hypothesis that parietal alpha causally suppresses the representation of contralateral space, steering spatial attention.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the spatial specificity of the stimulation effects.

claims.claim: Previous visual attention studies show that alpha-tACS increases endogenous alpha oscillations only when alpha power is low.
claims.source: First, previous visual attention studies show that alpha-tACS increases endogenous alpha oscillations only when alpha power is low (Alagapan et al., 2016; Neuling et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Top-down attention to the right should naturally produce strong rIPS alpha, limiting the influence of additional alpha power.
claims.source: Top-down attention to the right should naturally produce strong rIPS alpha, limiting the influence of additional alpha power (see Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on prior knowledge about alpha lateralization during spatial attention, depicted in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Intrinsic rIPS alpha power should be low during leftward attention, allowing stimulation to have an observable effect.
claims.source: In contrast, intrinsic rIPS alpha power should be low during leftward attention, allowing stimulation to have an observable effect.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on prior knowledge about alpha lateralization during spatial attention.

claims.claim: Parietal cortex is asymmetrical; rIPS predominantly represents left space, but also has a weak representation of right space.
claims.source: Second, parietal cortex is asymmetrical; rIPS predominantly represents left space, but also has a weak representation of right space.
claims.evidence: This is based on prior knowledge about hemispheric asymmetry in spatial representation.

claims.claim: When listeners attended to the right, an injection of alpha energy to rIPS may have enhanced suppression of the dominant leftward distractor, but it may also have spread to suppress the weak representation of the rightward target, leading to little net change.
claims.source: When listeners attended to the right, an injection of alpha energy to rIPS may have enhanced suppression of the dominant leftward distractor, but it may also have spread to suppress the weak representation of the rightward target, leading to little net change.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about why no effect was observed for rightward attention.

claims.claim: The results implicate parietal alpha in volitional steering of auditory spatial attention.
claims.source: Thus, our results implicate parietal alpha in volitional steering of auditory spatial attention.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the task-specificity and stimulus-specificity of the stimulation effects.

claims.claim: Schumann and colleagues found that parietal alpha stimulation caused a spatially specific effect in an endogenous attention task, decreasing reaction times for ipsilateral targets, but had no impact on exogenous attention or simple detection tasks.
claims.source: In this case, and only this case, parietal alpha stimulation caused a spatially specific effect, decreasing reaction times for ipsilateral targets.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Schuhmann, 2019).

claims.claim: While parietal alpha modulates volitional control of spatial attention tasks, it does not robustly influence exogenous attention.
claims.source: These findings highlight the importance of carefully considering task demands when interpreting results of parietal stimulation studies. While parietal alpha modulates volitional control of spatial attention tasks, it does not robustly influence exogenous attention.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of results across multiple studies, including Schuhmann (2019).

claims.claim: The sudden appearance of a new stimulus, even one near threshold, may draw exogenous attention, which may override any effects of parietal processing and render alpha parietal stimulation impotent.
claims.source: The sudden appearance of a new stimulus, even one near threshold, may draw exogenous attention (Desimone and Duncan, 1995), which may override any effects of parietal processing and render alpha parietal stimulation impotent (Brignani et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is speculation about why some studies failed to find effects of parietal stimulation, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Traditional tACS is usually delivered with large pads (5 × 5 cm2) and stimulates a broad area between the stimulation electrodes.
claims.source: Traditional tACS is usually delivered with large pads (5 × 5 cm2) and stimulates a broad area between the stimulation electrodes (Datta et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on tACS methodology.

claims.claim: The spread of electric current with traditional tACS is greater than with HD-tACS, and could even spread to both hemispheres, confounding stimulation effects.
claims.source: The resulting spread of electric current is greater, and could even spread to both hemispheres, confounding stimulation effects.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the known properties of traditional tACS.

claims.claim: The current study's HD-tACS stimulation targeted intraparietal sulcus and produces essentially no current in auditory sensory regions.
claims.source: In contrast to their study, our HD-tACS stimulation targeted intraparietal sulcus and produces essentially no current in auditory sensory regions (see Figure 8C).
claims.evidence: This is based on the current flow modeling shown in Figure 8C.

claims.claim: The current study demonstrates that alpha in IPS, which is a part of the well-studied visuo-spatial attention network, plays a causal role in spatial auditory attention.
claims.source: However, ours demonstrates that alpha in IPS, which is a part of the well-studied visuo-spatial attention network, plays a causal role in spatial auditory attention
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and the targeted stimulation location.

claims.claim: By including a nonspatial attention task as a control, the study shows that the influence of IPS alpha depends specifically on top-down engagement of the visuo-spatial attention network.
claims.source: By including a nonspatial attention task as a control, our study further shows that the influence of IPS alpha depends specifically on top-down engagement of the visuo-spatial attention network; there is no influence of IPS alpha stimulation when listeners attend to the same auditory source within the same physical sound mixture using nonspatial auditory features.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of stimulation effects during nonspatial attention.

claims.claim: Auditory spatial attention recruits the same fronto-parietal network involved in visual spatial attention.
claims.source: We believe that auditory spatial attention recruits the same fronto-parietal network involved in visual spatial attention (Michalka et al., 2016; see the discussion in Bonacci et al., 2019).

results.result: Talker discontinuity (switching trials) significantly disrupts spatial auditory attention performance compared to continuous trials, with performance dropping by approximately 20-25% for spatial attention tasks. This effect is larger than previously reported and is consistent across both the main and control experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C48 provide consistent statistical evidence across multiple conditions showing that switching trials significantly impair spatial attention performance (p<0.001 for most comparisons). The effect is replicated in both experiments and is larger than prior work (C49), which is explained by the more frequent talker switches in the current design. The statistical tests are appropriate and the results are internally consistent.

results.result: Alpha-frequency (10 Hz) HD-tACS of right parietal cortex specifically impairs leftward spatial auditory attention during continuous trials, with no effect on rightward attention. The effect is sustained throughout stimulation but disappears immediately after stimulation ends.
results.evaluation: Claims C53 and C58 provide direct statistical evidence (Z=2.10, p=0.036) for the primary hypothesis. Claims C56-C57 demonstrate temporal specificity through post-hoc analysis showing consistent effects during stimulation that rapidly dissipate. The effect size (0.33, C65) is comparable to other tACS studies. The spatial specificity (left but not right, C55) and rapid offset support a causal interpretation.

results.result: Parietal HD-tACS stimulation has no effect on nonspatial auditory attention tasks, even when analyzing performance by target location. Additionally, theta-frequency (6 Hz) stimulation has no effect on any task condition.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C60 provide statistical evidence showing no effects of stimulation during nonspatial attention (all p>0.095 for theta; p>0.19 for alpha nonspatial). This task-specificity and frequency-specificity (C64) strengthen the interpretation that alpha stimulation specifically affects spatial attention mechanisms. The control conditions are comprehensive and appropriately analyzed.

results.result: The effects of HD-tACS on auditory spatial attention do not persist after stimulation ends, with performance returning to baseline immediately in the post-stimulation block.
results.evaluation: Claims C57 and C90 provide converging evidence from both planned and post-hoc analyses showing no persistent effects. Figure 6 (referenced in C57, C90) shows that performance differences between Sham and Stimulation sessions disappear in the first post-stimulation sub-block. This temporal specificity supports online rather than plastic effects of stimulation.

results.result: The study demonstrates a causal, frequency-specific, hemisphere-specific, and task-specific role of parietal alpha oscillations in top-down control of auditory spatial attention, establishing that the visuo-spatial attention network in IPS causally controls auditory spatial attention.
results.evaluation: This overarching conclusion (C7, C62) is supported by the convergence of multiple specific findings: frequency specificity (alpha but not theta, C66), spatial specificity (left but not right attention affected by right hemisphere stimulation, C67), task specificity (spatial but not nonspatial attention, C73, C81), and anatomical specificity (IPS targeting, C80). The comprehensive control conditions and within-subject design support causal interpretation.

results.result: Baseline performance was equivalent between Sham and Stimulation sessions, and individual performance was stable across testing days, validating the within-subject experimental design.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C52 provide statistical validation of the experimental design. No baseline differences (p>0.65) confirm successful counterbalancing (C51), while significant test-retest correlations (rho~0.5, p<0.035) demonstrate stable individual differences. These methodological controls are essential for interpreting the stimulation effects.

results.result: The effect size of alpha HD-tACS on leftward spatial attention (d=0.33) is comparable to effect sizes reported in meta-analyses of tACS and tDCS studies on cognitive function.
results.evaluation: Claim C65 provides appropriate context by comparing the observed effect size to published meta-analytic estimates (0.36 for tACS, 0.23 for tDCS). The effect size calculation method is stated and the comparison suggests the finding is robust relative to the broader brain stimulation literature.

results.result: The lack of effect on rightward attention may be explained by ceiling effects (rIPS alpha already high during rightward attention) or by competing effects on weak ipsilateral and strong contralateral representations in the asymmetric parietal cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C72 provide plausible post-hoc explanations for the null result for rightward attention, citing prior literature on state-dependent tACS effects (C68) and hemispheric asymmetry (C71). However, these remain speculative interpretations (C72 explicitly labeled as speculation) rather than tested hypotheses. The reasoning is sound but lacks direct empirical support from the current study.

results.result: HD-tACS provides more spatially focused stimulation than traditional tACS, though current flow modeling shows non-uniform distribution within rIPS, with strongest stimulation in posterior regions (IPS1/2) rather than higher IPS regions most involved in auditory spatial attention.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 accurately describe HD-tACS methodology with appropriate citations. Claims C79, C85, C87 acknowledge limitations based on current flow modeling (Figure 8), noting that stimulation may not optimally target the most relevant IPS regions. This honest assessment of spatial precision is important for interpreting results and planning future studies.

results.result: The current findings align with recent visual attention studies showing that parietal alpha stimulation affects endogenous but not exogenous spatial attention, highlighting the importance of task demands in brain stimulation research.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C75 accurately summarize findings from Schuhmann (2019) showing task-dependent effects of parietal stimulation. Claim C84 demonstrates that the current auditory results parallel these visual findings. The interpretation (C76) about exogenous attention overriding parietal effects is speculative but well-supported by citations and consistent with the switching trial results.

results.result: The mechanisms of tACS effects and optimal stimulation parameters remain unclear. Future studies using individualized frequency matching, closed-loop approaches, or higher intensities may produce stronger or more persistent effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C89 cite prior work on potential tACS mechanisms (entrainment vs. membrane polarization). Claims C91-C95 are explicitly speculative suggestions for future work. While these are reasonable hypotheses supported by citations, they represent untested possibilities rather than established findings. The speculation is appropriately qualified.

results.result: The study included 38 participants (20 in main experiment, 18 in control) with normal hearing, recruited based on power analysis from pilot data estimating 14 subjects needed for adequate power.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C103 provide clear methodological details about participants and sample size determination. The power analysis (C102) is appropriate, though it only considered the two primary planned comparisons. The actual sample sizes (C99-C100, C103) exceed the estimated requirement, providing adequate power for the main hypotheses.

results.result: The auditory task used competing speech streams (5 syllables each) from male and female talkers, spatialized to left and right locations, with subjects counting target /ga/ syllables while ignoring distractors.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C109 provide detailed, verifiable descriptions of the experimental stimuli and task. The stimulus parameters (syllable types, durations, spatial positions, temporal structure) are clearly specified. The task design appropriately challenges selective attention while allowing objective performance measurement.

results.result: HD-tACS was delivered using a 5-electrode montage targeting right IPS, with 1.5 mA sinusoidal stimulation at 10 Hz (main experiment) or 6 Hz (control experiment), based on current flow modeling and prior literature on stimulation parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C122 provide comprehensive methodological details about the stimulation protocol. The electrode montage (C113-C114), stimulation parameters (C115-C118), and rationale for parameter choices (C116-C117, C119-C120) are clearly described with appropriate citations. The sham protocol (C122) is appropriate for blinding.

results.result: Subjects could not differentiate sham from active stimulation sessions in pilot testing, and prior studies using similar parameters found no better than chance discrimination.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C124 provide evidence for effective blinding, though the assessment in the current study was informal (verbal questioning in pilots). The citation to prior systematic assessments (C124) strengthens confidence in blinding effectiveness, though formal assessment in the main study would have been preferable.

results.result: Prior research establishes that both visual and auditory spatial attention produce lateralized parietal alpha activity, with alpha increasing ipsilateral to attention focus. Parietal cortex is involved in spatial but not nonspatial auditory attention, and brain stimulation studies suggest causal links between parietal alpha and visual spatial attention.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C20 accurately summarize prior literature with appropriate citations. The review establishes the foundation for the current study by documenting: (1) alpha lateralization during spatial attention in both modalities (C1, C13-C15), (2) parietal involvement in spatial but not nonspatial auditory attention (C17-C20), and (3) causal evidence from visual studies (C2). This provides strong motivation for testing causal effects in audition.

results.result: Prior research shows that feature continuity, particularly talker continuity, automatically influences auditory attention. Talker discontinuities disrupt both behavioral performance and parietal alpha lateralization during spatial attention tasks, suggesting that feature continuity can override volitional spatial attention control.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C26 accurately summarize prior behavioral and neural findings on feature continuity effects, with appropriate citations. The interpretation that talker continuity overrides top-down control (C26) is an inference from Mehraei et al. (2018) that motivated the switching trial manipulation in the current study. This provides strong rationale for including continuous vs. switching trials as a control.

results.result: Prior brain stimulation studies show mixed results for effects of parietal stimulation on visual spatial attention, with TMS and rTMS generally showing spatially specific effects, but tACS results being inconsistent. Recent HD-tACS studies show more promising results. Some studies have shown effects of stimulating auditory cortex on auditory attention.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C33 provide a balanced review of prior stimulation literature, acknowledging both positive findings (C27-C30, C32) and null results (C31). The citations are appropriate and the summary accurately represents the mixed state of the literature, providing context for why the current study using HD-tACS is needed. The mention of auditory cortex stimulation (C33) distinguishes the current parietal focus.

results.result: The study targeted right IPS based on hemispheric asymmetry in spatial representation, hypothesizing that alpha stimulation would impair leftward attention (primary hypothesis) and might improve or have no effect on rightward attention (secondary hypothesis).
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C39 clearly state the a priori hypotheses with appropriate citations for the rationale (C37). The primary hypothesis (C38) is directional and specific, while the secondary hypothesis (C39) appropriately acknowledges uncertainty about the direction of effect for rightward attention. This transparent statement of hypotheses is important for interpreting the statistical approach.

results.result: Traditional tACS uses large electrode pads and produces broader, less focal current spread than HD-tACS, potentially affecting both hemispheres and confounding results.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78 accurately describe limitations of traditional tACS with appropriate citations (C77). The inference about bilateral spread and confounding (C78) is reasonable based on the physics of current flow, though somewhat speculative. This provides context for why HD-tACS was chosen and why some prior tACS studies may have failed to find effects.

results.result: The authors hypothesize that auditory and visual spatial attention recruit the same fronto-parietal network and therefore should be similarly affected by parietal alpha manipulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C83 clearly state the authors' theoretical framework with supporting citations. This is presented as a belief/hypothesis (C82) rather than established fact, which is appropriate. The hypothesis is reasonable given the cited evidence and provides a clear theoretical motivation for expecting similar effects across modalities.

results.result: Abnormalities in parietal alpha have been documented in various clinical disorders, and studies manipulating parietal alpha may inform future therapeutic interventions.
results.evaluation: Claim C96 accurately cites clinical literature on alpha abnormalities in various disorders. However, claim C97's suggestion that this work lays groundwork for clinical interventions is speculative. While the logic is sound, the leap from basic research in healthy adults to clinical applications is substantial and would require extensive additional validation. The speculation is appropriately qualified but remains uncertain.

results.result: Testing sessions were separated by 1-16 days, and most subjects performed the task in darkness based on prior reports that alpha stimulation is more effective in darkness, with one exception due to claustrophobia.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C111 provide clear procedural details about session timing. Claims C125-C126 describe the lighting conditions with appropriate citation (C125) and transparent reporting of the single exception (C126). The rationale for darkness is reasonable though the supporting evidence is limited to one citation. The exception is appropriately documented.
